summary: This paper develops seam-measurement scheduling policies for distributed quantum error correction using triangular color codes partitioned across multiple QPUs connected by photonic links. The Skip-Seam-$\tau$ (SS-$\tau$) and Adaptive Skip-$\tau$ (AST) schemes reduce how often remote seam stabilizers are measured to balance Bell-pair generation delays against syndrome staleness, achieving lower logical error rates than the Measure-All baseline in identified parameter regimes.
motivation: In modular distributed QEC architectures, seam checks requiring non-local CNOTs via heralded Bell pairs are substantially slower and noisier than local bulk checks, accumulating idle decoherence while waiting for entanglement. The entanglement generation rate (EGR) creates an asymmetry not present in monolithic systems, motivating adaptive control of seam-measurement frequency to optimize performance.
method: The authors introduce a scheduling module that controls seam-check frequency independently of bulk checks in a distributed triangular color code ($d \in \{9, 15, 17, 21\}$) partitioned across four QPUs. SS-$\tau$ measures seam checks once every $\tau$ rounds with syndrome copying; AST adapts $\tau$ as $\tau^\star = (d-1)/2$ at low EGR and $\tau^\star = 2$ at high EGR. Simulations use Stim with circuit-level noise ($p = 10^{-3}$), two-qubit seam-gate error $10p$, and idle noise from Bell-pair wait times with $T_1 = 200$ µs, $T_2 = 150$ µs.
result: For $p = 10^{-3}$ and EGR in the range 31.6–70.7 MHz, both SS-$\tau$ and AST exhibit fault-tolerant distance scaling with logical error rate decreasing as code distance increases, significantly outperforming Measure-All and narrowing the gap with monolithic architectures. At fixed EGR = 50 MHz, AST reduces LER by larger margins at $d=19$ than $d=17$, demonstrating increasing benefit at larger distances.
